primitives.verbatim_quote: Now in most persons the internal recti muscles, to which convergence is due, are weaker than the others; and the entirely passive position of the eyeballs, the position which they assume when covered and looking at nothing in particular, is either that of parallelism or of slight divergence.

primitives.assumptions: Muscle asymmetry leads to a natural bias toward outward eye positioning in the absence of visual input.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Monocular viewing where the unoccluded eye must compensate for the occluded eye's divergent reset, leading to apparent motion.

layer2.mapping: GSI - Encodes passive misalignment as a systematic error term in stereo calibration. GSE - Uses divergence bias as a predictive feature for gaze prediction models.

primitives.name: Vergence Adaptation Latency
primitives.verbatim_quote: Make a person look with both eyes at some near object, and then screen the object from one of his eyes by a card or book.
primitives.assumptions: Neural processing delay exists before the occluded eye can re-converge upon removing the screen.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Transients where the occluded eye's reset lags behind the working eye's updated focus, creating momentary stereo mismatch.

layer2.mapping: GSI - Models adaptation latency as a hidden Markov state in dynamic belief networks. GSE - Incorporates temporal hysteresis into real-time rendering of binocular parallax.
layer2.telemetry: Time interval (ms) between screen removal and visible convergence response of the previously occluded eye

The core geometric principle is that binocular convergence forms a direct sensory-motor link to perceived depth. When one eye is occluded, the passive divergence of the unoccluded eye creates a baseline misalignment. Reopening the occluded eye forces a rapid vergence response to re-establish stereo correspondence, producing the illusion of depth change. This mechanism couples retinal disparity with muscular effort, making distance judgments inherently tied to motor states. The asymmetry in rectus muscle strength introduces a persistent bias that complicates accurate depth perception, especially in dynamic scenes.
